title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
shows: Defines RAG: a model that pulls passages from an external index at answer time instead of storing all knowledge in its weights.
takeaway: The core pattern we need: knowledge stays outside the model and is fetched at query time, so the brain can hold pointers and fetch live.

title: Seven Failure Points When Engineering a Retrieval Augmented Generation System
shows: Lists seven concrete places a RAG pipeline breaks, drawn from real case studies.
takeaway: Use the seven failure points as a test checklist for the brain's retrieval layer.

title: FACTS About Building Retrieval Augmented Generation-based Chatbots
shows: Describes lessons from building enterprise RAG chatbots, including honoring document access controls.
takeaway: Access control is a first-class design input for enterprise retrieval, not an add-on.

title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
shows: Models use information at the start and end of a long context better than the middle.
takeaway: Return few, well-ordered passages rather than dumping many hits into the prompt.

title: Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
shows: Trains a model to decide when to retrieve and to critique its own retrieved evidence.
takeaway: Let the caller decide whether to hit the index at all, and score evidence before use.

title: Adaptive-RAG: Learning to Adapt Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models through Question Complexity
shows: Routes each question to no retrieval, single-step, or multi-step retrieval based on its difficulty.
takeaway: Add a cheap router in front of the index so simple questions skip the expensive path.

title: Search-R1: Training LLMs to Reason and Leverage Search Engines with Reinforcement Learning
shows: Trains a model with reinforcement learning to issue its own search queries across multiple turns.
takeaway: The brain's query interface should be a tool that an agent can call repeatedly and refine.

title: Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey on Agentic RAG
shows: Surveys RAG systems where agents plan, pick tools and iterate on retrieval.
takeaway: Gives the vocabulary and patterns (routing, reflection, multi-agent) for the query layer.

title: Beyond Semantic Similarity: Rethinking Retrieval for Agentic Search via Direct Corpus Interaction
shows: Argues a single top-k similarity call hides evidence from agents and lets them work on the corpus directly with exact and multi-step operations.
takeaway: Support exact and structured lookups against source systems alongside the semantic index; do not rely on top-k alone.

title: From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization
shows: Builds an entity graph and community summaries from documents to answer whole-corpus questions plain vector RAG cannot.
takeaway: An entity and relationship layer across apps (person, project, ticket) answers cross-app questions; keep it as links back to sources.

title: HippoRAG: Neurobiologically Inspired Long-Term Memory for Large Language Models
shows: Combines an LLM-built knowledge graph with personalized PageRank to connect facts across documents in one retrieval step.
takeaway: Graph walks over pointers can link evidence across Slack, Jira and docs without copying their text.

title: From RAG to Memory: Non-Parametric Continual Learning for Large Language Models
shows: Extends HippoRAG to improve factual, sense-making and associative memory tasks while staying non-parametric.
takeaway: Shows an external, updatable index can serve as continual memory without retraining a model.

title: LightRAG: Simple and Fast Retrieval-Augmented Generation
shows: Graph-based RAG with two-level (entity and theme) retrieval that supports incremental updates.
takeaway: Incremental graph updates are the pattern to copy so new events do not force a full re-index.

title: MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems
shows: Treats LLM context like an OS with paging between a small working memory and external storage.
takeaway: Model the brain as external memory the agent pages in on demand.

title: A-MEM: Agentic Memory for LLM Agents
shows: Memory notes that the agent links and updates itself, in a Zettelkasten style.
takeaway: Index entries can carry self-maintained links and updates, which supports self-updating behavior.

title: Mem0: Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory
shows: Extracts, consolidates and retrieves salient facts from conversations for long-term agent memory, with a graph variant.
takeaway: Store distilled facts with provenance rather than full transcripts; consolidate on write.

title: Zep: A Temporal Knowledge Graph Architecture for Agent Memory
shows: A temporal knowledge graph that tracks when facts were true and merges conversation and business data.
takeaway: Give every index fact a validity time so superseded facts are not served as current.

title: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
shows: Agents keep a memory stream and retrieve by recency, importance and relevance.
takeaway: Rank index hits by recency and importance as well as similarity.

title: Memory in the Age of AI Agents
shows: Survey that organizes the fragmented agent-memory field into a clearer taxonomy.
takeaway: Use its taxonomy to scope what the brain stores versus what each agent keeps privately.

title: Anatomy of Agentic Memory: Taxonomy and Empirical Analysis of Evaluation and System Limitations
shows: Finds agent-memory benchmarks underscaled, metrics misaligned and system costs often ignored.
takeaway: Measure cost and latency of memory operations, not only answer accuracy.

title: PLAID: An Efficient Engine for Late Interaction Retrieval
shows: Makes ColBERT-style late-interaction retrieval much faster via centroid-based pruning.
takeaway: Late interaction gives high-precision matching; its larger index is a cost to weigh against single-vector indexes.

title: FreshDiskANN: A Fast and Accurate Graph-Based ANN Index for Streaming Similarity Search
shows: A disk-based graph index that supports inserts and deletes while serving queries.
takeaway: Direct evidence that a vector index can stay fresh from a change stream without full rebuilds.

title: SPANN: Highly-efficient Billion-scale Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
shows: Keeps centroids in memory and posting lists on disk to search billions of vectors cheaply.
takeaway: Pointer-sized entries plus disk-resident detail is a workable cost model for a company-wide index.

title: ACORN: Performant and Predicate-Agnostic Search Over Vector Embeddings and Structured Data
shows: Vector search that works with arbitrary metadata filters without building one index per filter.
takeaway: Permission and source filters must run inside the ANN search, not after it.

title: Recall-Bounded Staleness for Filtered Multi-Tenant ANN Graph Indexes under Concurrent Updates
shows: Combines streaming updates, metadata filtering and multi-tenancy in one graph index and bounds the recall lost during updates.
takeaway: Matches our exact need: multi-tenant, filtered, continuously updated. Treat as a design reference; it is a new single-author preprint.

title: Toward Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Enterprise Retail Workflows over Heterogeneous Data Sources
shows: Introduces RetailBridge, a benchmark where agents must pick sources and carry evidence between structured and unstructured data.
takeaway: Source selection and cross-source evidence chaining are the hard part; test the brain on that explicitly.

title: UniMS-RAG: A Unified Multi-source Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Personalized Dialogue Systems
shows: One model plans which knowledge source to use, retrieves from it, and generates the answer.
takeaway: A planner step that picks the source before retrieval is a proven pattern for multi-source routing.

title: PoisonedRAG: Knowledge Corruption Attacks to Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
shows: Shows that inserting a few crafted texts into the knowledge base can steer RAG answers.
takeaway: Anyone who can write to a connected app can influence the brain; record source trust and author with each pointer.

title: Not what you've signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection
shows: Retrieved content can carry hidden instructions that hijack an LLM-integrated app.
takeaway: Treat all fetched source content as untrusted data, never as instructions.

title: Text Embeddings Reveal (Almost) As Much As Text
shows: Reconstructs much of the original text from its embedding vector.
takeaway: Embeddings are not safe to treat as anonymized; protect and permission the index as if it held the text.

title: The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
shows: Shows RAG databases can leak private data through the model's answers.
takeaway: Enforce access checks before content reaches the model, since output filtering alone will leak.

title: Benchmarking Knowledge-Extraction Attack and Defense on Retrieval-Augmented Generation
shows: A systematic benchmark of attacks that extract knowledge-base content through crafted queries, with defenses.
takeaway: Rate-limit and audit query patterns; test the brain against extraction attacks.

title: Enterprise AI Must Enforce Participant-Aware Access Control
shows: Demonstrates data exfiltration from enterprise assistants and argues access control must consider every participant in a conversation.
takeaway: Authorize against the full set of people in the session, not just the asker.

title: Securing the Agent: Vendor-Neutral, Multitenant Enterprise Retrieval and Tool Use
shows: Points out that retrieval ranks by relevance, not authorization, so one tenant's query can surface another's data.
takeaway: Make authorization a filter inside retrieval, evaluated per query with the user's live permissions.

title: Enterprise-Grade Security for the Model Context Protocol (MCP): Frameworks and Mitigation Strategies
shows: Threat model and mitigations for MCP, the protocol agents use to reach external tools and data.
takeaway: If live fetch goes through MCP-style connectors, adopt its threat model: scoped tokens, tool allowlists, audit.

title: Auditing MCP Servers for Over-Privileged Tool Capabilities
shows: A toolkit that finds MCP servers exposing risky capabilities such as file, network and command access.
takeaway: Audit each connector for least privilege before it joins the brain.

title: Ragas: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation
shows: Reference-free metrics for retrieval relevance, faithfulness and answer relevance.
takeaway: Gives cheap automatic metrics we can run continuously on the brain.

title: CRAG -- Comprehensive RAG Benchmark
shows: A benchmark with questions of varying popularity and how fast their answers change, plus mock search APIs.
takeaway: Use its dynamism categories as a model for freshness test sets.

title: FreshLLMs: Refreshing Large Language Models with Search Engine Augmentation
shows: Introduces FreshQA for fast-changing facts and shows that fresh retrieved evidence improves answers.
takeaway: Build a freshness test set from our own apps: change a fact, measure time until the brain answers correctly.

title: Stale-Document Poisoning: When Outdated Retrieval Overrides Correct Model Answers
shows: Builds 317 verified knowledge reversals and shows outdated retrieved evidence can make a model wrong where it was right without retrieval.
takeaway: Stale index entries can be worse than no index; verify freshness at fetch time before answering.

title: Temporal Validity in Retrieval Memory: Eliminating Stale-Fact Errors for AI Agents over Evolving Knowledge
shows: Shows embedding similarity cannot tell a contradicted fact from a duplicate (AUROC 0.59) and proposes temporal handling.
takeaway: Store version and supersession links explicitly; do not trust similarity to resolve conflicts.

title: Case-Aware LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluation for Enterprise-Scale RAG Systems
shows: An evaluation framework for multi-turn enterprise RAG that catches case misidentification and partial resolution.
takeaway: Evaluate multi-turn, identifier-heavy enterprise tasks, not just single-shot QA.

title: Policy-aware Vector Search: A Vision for Fine Grained Access Control in Vector Databases
shows: Vector databases lack fine-grained access control, and enforcing it trades off policy correctness, nearest-neighbor recall and latency. The paper formalizes the problem and compares enforcement strategies.
takeaway: Enforce permissions inside the retrieval call, and measure recall and latency under each user's policy, instead of trusting a post-filter.

title: Towards Secure Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Comprehensive Review of Threats, Defenses and Benchmarks
shows: An end-to-end survey of RAG security. It groups threats such as poisoning and membership inference, and defenses such as access control, encrypted retrieval and differential privacy.
takeaway: Use this survey as the checklist for threat coverage, and map each pointer-store control to one of its defense stages.

title: Defeating Prompt Injections by Design
who: Debenedetti et al., Google, ETH Zurich
shows: CaMeL separates trusted control flow from untrusted data and uses capabilities on tool calls. It solves 77% of AgentDojo tasks with provable security, against 84% undefended.
takeaway: Keep the planner away from retrieved content and attach capabilities to every pointer, so a poisoned document cannot steer tool calls.

title: Adaptive Evaluation of Out-of-Band Defenses Against Prompt Injection in LLM Agents
shows: Treats CaMeL, FIDES and Progent as policy enforcement outside the model. A small test on a weak model found one adaptive attack barely helped, but stronger attacks are untested.
takeaway: Put authorization in deterministic code outside the model, and plan adaptive red-team tests before claiming the brain is injection-safe.

title: Can CaMeLs Talk? Securing Multi-Agent Systems Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks
shows: CaMeL guarantees do not compose when agents call other agents. An attack works even if each agent runs CaMeL. A provenance-tracking agent protocol cut attack success to 0.0%.
takeaway: Carry trust labels across agent-to-agent calls to the brain, since a downstream agent may treat untrusted data as trusted input.

title: Indirect Prompt Injections: Are Firewalls All You Need, or Stronger Benchmarks?
shows: Input and output firewalls at the tool boundary scored near-perfect on four public benchmarks, but the authors show those benchmarks have weak attacks and flawed metrics.
takeaway: Filter at the tool boundary as one layer, but do not trust benchmark scores alone; test with adaptive and second-order attacks.

title: MCPTox: A Benchmark for Tool Poisoning Attack on Real-World MCP Servers
shows: Hidden instructions in MCP tool metadata fooled many agents. The top attack success rate was 72.8%, more capable models were often more vulnerable, and refusals stayed under 3%.
takeaway: Treat third-party tool descriptions as untrusted input, pin and review them, and never let metadata widen what a tool may reach.

title: When the Manual Lies: A Realistic Benchmark to Evaluate MCP Poisoning Attacks for LLM Agents
shows: A 32-case benchmark of tool description poisoning showed very high attack success on several models, and prompt-based guardrails were largely ineffective and sometimes made things worse.
takeaway: Do not rely on prompt guardrails for tool safety; enforce allowed actions in code and log every tool call.

title: Riddle Me This! Stealthy Membership Inference for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
shows: Natural-sounding queries, about 30 per document, can tell whether a specific document sits in a RAG datastore, and are harder to detect than earlier attacks.
takeaway: Even a yes or no answer can leak that a document exists, so hide existence of pointers the caller may not see.

title: Zero2Text: Zero-Training Cross-Domain Inversion Attacks on Textual Embeddings
shows: A training-free, black-box attack rebuilds text from embeddings, including from unfamiliar domains, and the authors report that differential privacy defenses do not stop it.
takeaway: Treat stored embeddings as sensitive as the source text; keep vectors in the owning system or encrypt them, and do not copy them centrally.

title: Embedding Inference Attack
shows: Queries seeing only the unordered set of retrieved documents can reveal which embedding model a system uses, even with a reranker added.
takeaway: Do not assume that hiding scores hides the retrieval setup; expose only what each caller needs and rate-limit probing.

title: Unveiling Privacy Risks in LLM Agent Memory
shows: MEXTRA is a black-box attack that pulls private records out of an agent's memory with crafted prompts, and works across two agents and attacker knowledge levels.
takeaway: Give each user a separate memory store, and treat agent memory as a retrieval surface that needs the same access checks as documents.

title: Topology Matters: Measuring Memory Leakage in Multi-Agent LLMs
shows: Private data leaks more when agents are densely connected, close to the attacker, or central. Sparse or hierarchical links leak less. Accepted to Findings of ACL 2026.
takeaway: Keep the agent graph sparse and hierarchical, and add access control per link rather than one shared pool.

title: No Attacker Needed: Unintentional Cross-User Contamination in Shared-State LLM Agents
shows: With raw shared state, ordinary use alone contaminated other users at 57 to 71%. Write-time cleaning helped for chat text but not for executable artifacts.
takeaway: Scope every stored fact to its owner and context, and do not rely on text sanitization for saved code or tool outputs.

title: PiSAs: Benchmarking Contextual Integrity in Multi-User Agentic Systems
shows: A benchmark of cross-user leakage across outputs, agent messages and memory found that even top models do not reliably limit sharing to authorized users.
takeaway: Do not let the model decide who may see what; check the audience in code before any content reaches a user or another agent.

title: AIM: A Privacy-Aware Interoperable Memory Framework for Multi-Agent Multi-User LLM Systems
shows: AIM labels memories private or public and uses index-level access control. It reports 96.0% visibility accuracy but only 58.8% strict operation accuracy on its benchmark.
takeaway: Use owner-scoped index access for memory, but expect write and update errors, so audit memory operations and make deletes verifiable.

title: Efficient Federated Search for Retrieval-Augmented Generation using Lightweight Routing
shows: A small classifier picks which sources to query per question, cutting communication by up to 80.65% and latency by up to 52.50% with accuracy near querying every source.
takeaway: Put a cheap learned source router in front of live fetch so most questions touch only a few connected apps.

title: DFAMS: Dynamic-flow guided Federated Alignment based Multi-prototype Search
shows: Uses signals inside the LLM to detect query intent and route across heterogeneous knowledge partitions, beating prior federated retrieval by up to 6.45% in answer accuracy.
takeaway: Routing ambiguous cross-domain questions benefits from learned intent signals, so plan to train or tune the router on our own query logs.

title: Federated Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Systematic Mapping Study
shows: Maps federated RAG work from 2020 to 2025 and flags privacy, client differences and weak evaluation as persistent open problems.
takeaway: Expect no ready benchmark for pointer-based federation; build our own evaluation covering source differences and privacy.

title: LiveVectorLake: A Real-Time Versioned Knowledge Base Architecture for Streaming Vector Updates and Temporal Retrieval
shows: Chunk-level hash change detection re-processed only about 10 to 15% of content per update on a small 100-document test, with a hot index and a versioned history store.
takeaway: Detect changes per chunk and keep a current tier plus version history; the test is tiny, so treat the numbers as a hint only.

title: From Static to Dynamic: A Streaming RAG Approach to Real-time Knowledge Base
shows: Keeps a compact set of prototype vectors refreshed during queries, reporting under 15 ms latency and over 900 documents per second within 150 MB.
takeaway: A small hot index can follow a change stream without blocking queries; verify on our own event volume before relying on it.

title: In-Place Updates of a Graph Index for Streaming Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
shows: Handles each insert and delete in place instead of batch consolidation, keeping recall stable over long update sequences.
takeaway: Choose a vector index that deletes in place, so removed or revoked documents leave search results quickly.

title: EMA: Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search with General Attribute Filtering and Dynamic Updates
shows: Filtered vector search over mixed numeric and categorical attributes with dynamic updates, reporting 1.68x to 12.25x speedup over general filtering methods.
takeaway: Permission, source and date filters can run inside updatable ANN search; benchmark this class of index for the pointer store.

title: From BM25 to Corrective RAG: Benchmarking Retrieval Strategies for Text-and-Table Documents
shows: On 23,088 financial queries, hybrid retrieval plus neural reranking was best (Recall@5 0.816), BM25 beat dense retrieval, and contextual retrieval gave steady gains.
takeaway: Ship hybrid lexical plus dense search with a reranker, and keep exact-match search for identifiers and numbers.

title: RECON: Benchmarking Agent Memory for Compositional Reasoning over Long Contexts
shows: A benchmark of 24 long case files where the best non-oracle system reaches only 22.4% accuracy at tracing how changed evidence affects conclusions.
takeaway: Retrieval alone will not handle changed facts that ripple downstream; add explicit supersession checks and test for them.

title: AgenticRAG: Agentic Retrieval for Enterprise Knowledge Bases
shows: An agent with search, find, open and summarize tools over existing enterprise search reports 92% correctness on FinanceBench, and tool use gave a 5.9x ablation gain.
takeaway: Expose the brain as a few simple tools an agent calls in a loop rather than one retrieval call.

title: Keyword search is all you need: Achieving RAG-Level Performance without vector databases using agentic tool use
shows: Agents with only keyword search tools reach over 90% of the performance of traditional RAG, with no persistent vector database.
takeaway: Live keyword calls to source APIs can be a strong baseline; test them against our index before paying for full embedding copies.

title: LiveMCPBench: Can Agents Navigate an Ocean of MCP Tools?
shows: On 95 tasks over 70 MCP servers and 527 tools, most models scored 30 to 50% success, and retrieval errors caused nearly half of failures.
takeaway: Picking the right connector tool is the bottleneck; keep a searchable catalog of tools and limit how many an agent sees.

title: MCP-Atlas: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Tool-Use Competency with Real MCP Servers
shows: 1,000 tasks over 36 real MCP servers; the best pass rate was 82.2%, and 63.3% of diagnosed failures were reasoning failures, not tool-call errors.
takeaway: Multi-server chaining fails mostly in planning, so the brain should return clear, structured results that make the next step obvious.

title: Benchmarking Deep Search over Heterogeneous Enterprise Data
shows: A benchmark over 39,190 artifacts from documents, transcripts, Slack and GitHub; the best agentic RAG method averages 32.96, with retrieval as the main bottleneck.
takeaway: Cross-app multi-hop questions are hard today; use this benchmark style, including unanswerable questions, as our acceptance test.

title: DRBench: A Realistic Benchmark for Enterprise Deep Research
shows: 100 open-ended tasks across 10 domains that need facts from both the public web and private email, chat and cloud files.
takeaway: Test the brain on report-style tasks that mix private and public sources, not just short factual questions.

title: Evaluating Long-Horizon Memory for Multi-Party Collaborative Dialogues
shows: A benchmark of multi-party, million-token team conversations where current memory systems fail on multi-hop questions and on time reasoning without explicit version information.
takeaway: Store version and supersession data on every fact, and test the brain on multi-person team threads, not only one-on-one chat.

title: Locomo-Plus: Beyond-Factual Cognitive Memory Evaluation Framework for LLM Agents
shows: Finds that older memory benchmarks mostly test explicit fact recall, and that remembering unstated goals or constraints is much harder for current memory systems.
takeaway: Do not judge the brain only on fact lookup; add tests for constraints and preferences that a query does not mention directly.

title: A Simple Yet Strong Baseline for Long-Term Conversational Memory of LLM Agents
shows: Splits each chat session into standalone, entity-normalized statements linked in a graph, matching strong baselines on LoCoMo and LongMemEval_S with much shorter answer contexts.
takeaway: Index small entity-normalized statements that point back to the source message, rather than whole transcripts or lossy summaries.

title: SWE-chat: Coding Agent Interactions From Real Users in the Wild
shows: A dataset of nearly 18,000 real coding-agent sessions showing only 59% of agent code survives into commits and users push back in about half of turns.
takeaway: Session logs carry strong signals such as pushback and rework; mine those as pointers to lessons instead of treating every turn as knowledge.

title: CODESKILL: Learning Self-Evolving Skills for Coding Agents
shows: Trains a model to extract reusable skills from coding-agent trajectories and prune the skill bank, improving success on three coding benchmarks over a no-skill baseline.
takeaway: Extraction from agent sessions can pay off, but keep the skill bank small and score each skill by outcome before sharing it company-wide.

title: SPEM: Structure-Aware Procedural Memory for Efficient Skill Use in LLM Agents
shows: Stores single skills plus reusable skill compositions from successful runs, and picks between them with a graph selector that accounts for dependencies.
takeaway: Link skills to their prerequisites and to the sessions they came from, so a retrieved skill arrives with its context.

title: Can Agents Forget When Asked? A Benchmark for Memory Unlearning in LLM Agents
shows: Six memory systems completed at most 1.5% of forget requests end to end, leaving data extractable or deleting far more than asked.
takeaway: Do not trust a memory layer's delete call; build deletion as a tested workflow and probe for the data afterward.

title: Forgetting Without Restarting: Execution-State Unlearning for Stateful LLM Agents
shows: Deleting a memory record leaves summaries, plans and caches that still carry the data; replaying only the affected part matched a full reset at up to 9x fewer tokens.
takeaway: Record which derived items came from each source so a deletion can find and rebuild every dependent summary, not just the original pointer.

title: AfterDeleteBench: Auditing Post-Deletion Information Persistence in LLM Agents
shows: A single query often recovers a deleted secret from derived data like summaries, while provenance-aware controls removed the observed recovery and a literal write filter did not.
takeaway: Track provenance for every derived record and run a post-deletion audit query as part of each right-to-be-forgotten request.

title: Can Agents Truly Forget? Explore Machine Unlearning for LLM Agents
shows: Forgetting inside model weights is not enough, because stored memory or tool calls can bring the data back; current methods leave a gap at the whole-agent level.
takeaway: A deleted fact can return through a live fetch from the source app, so deletion must also be honored at the source and in cached results.

title: Ghost Vectors: Soft-Deleted Embeddings Remain Reconstructible in HNSW Vector Databases
shows: Soft-deleted vectors stay in HNSW index files and can be inverted to recover personal details; encrypting vectors and discarding the key on delete removed the observed recovery.
takeaway: A tombstone flag is not erasure; encrypt index entries per record or per epoch so deletion can be proven by destroying a key.

title: A Survey on Long-Term Memory Security in LLM Agents: Attacks, Defenses, and Governance Across the Memory Lifecycle
shows: Argues that retrieval-time fixes are not enough and proposes governance built on storage-time provenance, versioning and retention policies.
takeaway: Set provenance, versioning and a retention rule when an entry is written, since they are hard to add after the fact.

title: Entity Resolution in Practice: Lessons from a Self-Serve Pipeline
shows: Across six datasets no single matching method wins, precision and recall need different fixes, and one wrong link can chain many unrelated records together.
takeaway: Keep identity links reversible and re-check any merge across groups, because one bad person or project merge can contaminate many pointers.

title: LLM-Powered Knowledge Graphs for Enterprise Intelligence and Analytics
shows: Proposes an LLM framework that merges emails, calendars, chats, documents and logs into one activity-centered graph, and reports gains in expertise finding and task management.
takeaway: An activity graph across apps is a plausible route to expertise finding; treat the reported gains as unproven until tested on our own data.

title: A Qualitative Study of User Perception of M365 AI Copilot
shows: Interviews with 27 people after a six-month trial found value in retrieval and summaries, but concerns about privacy, transparency and bias, and a need for human review.
takeaway: Show users where each answer came from and what the brain can see; transparency is a trust feature, not decoration.

title: Generative AI in Knowledge Work: Perception, Usefulness, and Acceptance of Microsoft 365 Copilot
shows: Repeated employee surveys at a research organization found most value in structured, text-based tasks, with staff groups rating usefulness differently over time.
takeaway: Pilot with different roles separately and re-measure over months, since early opinions shift with use.
